title: AI's '7' Problem: How Large Language Models Got Stuck in a Groupthink Groove
summary: Open your favorite chatbot and type: 'Give me a random number between 1 and 10.' If it says 7, don't be surprised. Try again, and you'll likely get 3, 4, 8, or 9. This isn't a parlor trick—it's a symptom of a widespread AI ailment: groupthink. Large language models (LLMs) are far more predictable and less creative than most users realize. For coding or factual queries, that's fine. But for open-ended tasks like brainstorming a vacation or a band name, it's a creativity killer. Australian startup Springboards aims to fix this with Flint, an LLM trained to produce a wider variety of responses. 'Most language models are fighting hallucinations,' says CEO Pip Bingemann. 'We welcome them.' In a demo, when ChatGPT and Claude both named Toyota or Honda as a car type, Flint offered a Ford F-150. For a New Balance tagline, the first two said 'Run your way'; Flint generated 'Built to last, run to win.' This homogeneity was spotlighted in a NeurIPS award-winning paper, 'Artificial Hivemind,' which found that 25 different LLMs overwhelmingly produced 'Time is a river' when asked for a metaphor about time. The researchers suspect the cause is similar training data and objectives. Springboards' CTO Kieran Browne notes that chat interfaces mask this repetition, making users feel they're getting a personal response when they're actually receiving the same generic output as everyone else. Flint is integrated into Springboards' creative tool, where users can mix outputs from multiple models. By deliberately pushing for novelty, Flint offers an antidote to AI's '7' problem—though it may sometimes sacrifice reliability for originality. As AI becomes a go-to brainstorming partner, models that dare to be different could become essential.
why_it_matters: For young people using AI to brainstorm for school projects or creative writing, groupthink could limit originality and lead to generic ideas, so a model that deliberately pushes for variety helps preserve human creativity.

background_read: ChatGPT (made by OpenAI) and Claude (from Anthropic) are two of the most widely used conversational AI models, often serving as everyday brainstorming partners. NeurIPS (Neural Information Processing Systems) is a top‑tier annual conference where researchers present cutting‑edge AI work; winning an award there signals a study is highly influential. The ‘7’ problem is more than a quirk: it points to a deeper issue of ‘groupthink’ in AI, where models trained on similar internet text and with similar goals end up giving nearly identical answers, stifling diversity. This can reinforce existing biases and limit the range of creative possibilities. Springboards, the Australian startup behind Flint, argues that deliberately chasing novelty—even if it means more unpredictable or hallucinated outputs—can break the mold and restore creativity to human‑AI collaboration.

perspectives.description: Flint’s willingness to generate unusual, even wild, options helps users break out of mental ruts and discover ideas they might never have considered.
Deliberately welcoming hallucinations can make the model less trustworthy. In serious tasks, a factual error dressed up as a creative suggestion could mislead or cause harm.
The ‘7’ problem reflects a deeper conditioning: most LLMs are optimised to be safe and agreeable, which subtly narrows the range of possible outputs and mirrors training‑data biases.

If more companies build models that prioritise novelty, we might see a new generation of AI co‑creators. The challenge will be finding the right balance between creativity and factual reliability, possibly offering users a slider to dial between the two.
